boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Prenzlau entry (capitulation, 28 October 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: Murat's cavalry, Lasalle's, Grouchy's and Beaumont's troops with Milhaud's following, against Prince Hohenlohe's column at Prenzlau, from its arrival before the town to the capitulation in the position behind it. Prince August's battalion, cut off and taken separately, and the King's letter that reached Stettin after the capitulation are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart prints no strength for either side. His entry counts the Prussian army under General of Infantry Prince Hohenlohe only by the 10,000 men (among them 400 officers) who went into captivity under the capitulation (claim side-b-losses). By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner's table of the troops that capitulated and the French reports give other figures (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 28/10. capitulation of Prenzlau'; 'the French under Grand Duke Murat force the Prussian army under General of Infantry Prince Hohenlohe to capitulate, whereby 10,000 men (among them 400 officers) went into captivity, and 45 flags, 64 guns and 1,800 horses fell into the hands of the French'.

claims.value: Side B in Höpfner: his table of the troops that capitulated, from the Guard through grenadier and line infantry, cuirassiers and dragoons to the artillery, totals 300 officers, 8831 men and 1616 horses, with no figure for some units; counting the units whose strength could not be found, he puts the whole that fell to the enemy by the capitulation itself at probably not over 10,000 men and 1800 horses. He gives separately the King's regiment, 25 officers and 701 men when it fell into the enemy's power in the suburb, and the grenadier company Taubenheim, 3 officers and 138 men. Colonel Massenbach urged on the Prince that only pride and ambition could sacrifice the 7—8000 men still under his command.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 189 and 196-197; each column of the table adds up to its printed total, the entries printed '?' left out (our arithmetic). The table counts the troops that capitulated, at the outcome: it leaves out the units taken in the suburb before the capitulation, which Höpfner gives separately, the many officers who escaped to Stettin with or without detachments, and Prince August's battalion, cut off and forced to surrender separately by Murat's account, so it is neither the strength at the start of the engagement nor a full loss figure; the claim is tagged unresolved. Massenbach's figure is his own plea, not a count; it follows his report, which Höpfner quotes from Massenbach's memoir. English renderings (ours): 'there capitulated: 1st battalion of the Guard | 19 officers | 606 men'; '½ grenadier battalion Rabiel | 8 ditto | 315 ditto'; 'remains of the infantry regiment Braunschweig | ? ditto | 300 ditto'; 'ditto ditto infantry regiment Hohenlohe | ? ditto | ? ditto'; 'Leib cuirassier regiment | 25 ditto | 400 ditto | 400 horses'; 'dragoon regiment Prittwitz | 19 ditto | 258 ditto | 255 ditto'; 'horse battery Neander | 2 ditto | 170 ditto | 229 ditto'; '[total] | 300 officers | 8831 men | 1616 horses, so that, counting the units for which no statement of strength could be obtained, in all probably not over'; '10,000 men and 1800 horses fell into the enemy's hands through the capitulation itself'; 'the King's regiment numbered 25 officers and 701 men when it fell into the enemy's power in the suburb of Prenzlau; the grenadier company Taubenheim 3 officers 138 men'; 'he added: only pride and ambition could let the Prince sacrifice the 7—8000 men whom he still had under his command'; 'verbatim extract from Massenbach's historical' (OCR); 'while a crowd of officers, alone and with detachments, took the road to Löcknitz and escaped safely to Stettin' (OCR); Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. claims.value: Side B, side A's figures: General Milhaud reported from Boitzenburg on 28 October that he had again been assured that 18,000 infantry and 36 guns had passed, on and beside the road from Boitzenburg to Prenzlow. Murat wrote to the Emperor that 16,000 infantry and 6 regiments of cavalry had filed past his cavalry, and gave the result of the day as 16,000 infantry, 6 regiments of cavalry, 60 guns, 60 flags, the princes Auguste-Ferdinand, Hohenlohe and Tauenzien and several other generals. Höpfner gives the French reports as 16,000 infantry, 6 regiments of cavalry, 45 flags and 64 horsed guns, and adds that besides the regimental guns 30 guns were actually handed over or taken, so that the figure above may well be right.
claims.rationale: Side A's reports, read from the page images: Milhaud's figure came from informants before the action, Murat's are his count of the result; neither is reconciled with Höpfner's table (claim side-b-strength). Bodart's 45 flags and 64 guns are the figures Höpfner attributes to the French reports, not the 60 and 60 of Murat's letter read here; which French report Höpfner used was not checked, nor which figure his 'obige Zahl' means. English renderings (ours): Milhaud, 'General Milhaud to the Grand Duke of Berg. Boitzenburg, 28 October 1806'; 'I have just been assured again that 18,000 infantry and 36 guns had passed, half on the road from Boitzenburg to Prenzlow, half in the fields between the river and the high road'; Murat, as in claim side-b-strength for the heading and date; '16,000 infantry and 6 regiments of cavalry have filed past Your Majesty's cavalry'; 'Sire, 16,000 infantry, 6 regiments of cavalry, 60 guns, 60 flags, the princes Auguste-Ferdinand, Hohenlohe, Tauenzien and several other general officers are the result of this brilliant day'; Höpfner, 'the reports of the French speak of 16,000 men of infantry, 6 regiments of cavalry, 45 flags, 64 horsed guns. Besides the regimental guns, 30 guns were in reality handed over or taken, so the figure above may well be right'.

claims.value: Side A: Murat marched at 6 in the morning with all the cavalry to support General Lasalle, whose hussars had reached Prenzlau with the head of the Prussian column; General Milhaud followed the enemy with the 13th chasseurs and the 9th dragoons. Murat had Lasalle attack the suburb, supported by 6 guns, Grouchy's division and 3 regiments of Beaumont's division, and sent his aide de camp General Beaumont over the bridge at Gollmitz with a brigade of dragoons of Beaumont's division against the enemy's rear and flank. Grouchy brought up his 3 brigades at a fast trot. Höpfner: about 800 dragoons formed up with their backs to the barns of Prenzlau during the parley; Captain Taubenheim reported enemy voltigeurs, which would suggest some of Lannes's light infantry, and the enemy light infantry that came over the low town wall may have been the heads of the advance guard of Lannes's corps under General Suchet. No passage read gives a headcount for side A, and Bodart prints none.
claims.rationale: Murat's and Grouchy's letters and Höpfner's figures from the page images, Taubenheim's report from the OCR. English renderings (ours): Murat, as in claim side-b-strength for the heading and date; 'suspecting the movement I had ordered General Lasalle to go to Prenzlow in the night; the 2 heads of column arrived together at that town; the hussars had to do the honours and let the Prussian column pass'; 'at 6 o'clock in the morning I was on the march with all the cavalry to support General Lasalle. General Milhaud was following the enemy with the 13th chasseurs and the 9th dragoons'; 'I ordered General Lasalle to come up on the suburb and attack. I had him supported by 6 guns and by Grouchy's division and by 3 regiments of Beaumont's division'; 'General Beaumont, my aide de camp, was ordered to cross the bridge at the village of Gollmitz with a brigade of dragoons of Beaumont's division, to go and threaten and attack the rear and flank of the enemy'; Grouchy, 'General Grouchy to the Grand Duke of Berg. Baumgarten, 28 October 1806'; 'accordingly bringing up my 3 brigades at a fast trot, I deployed them in echelons within cannon range of Prenzlow, in accordance with Your Imperial Highness's intentions, so as to cut off, by charging Prince Hohenlohe's column, all that had not entered the town, and by a simultaneous and bold effort to try to enter it at the same time as those enemy troops that were able to withdraw into it'; Höpfner, 'immediately afterwards about 800 dragoons formed up with their backs to the barns of Prenzlau'; 'Captain Taubenheim claims in his report also to have had to do with enemy voltigeurs, which would suggest the presence of some light infantry of Marshal Lannes' (OCR); 'Captain Brünnow says in his report that he began the retreat from the Berliner-' (OCR); 'Thor only when the enemy light infantry had already entered over the low town wall and the barrier'; 'these may well have been the heads of the advance guard of Lannes's corps under General Suchet'.

claims.value: Bodart names Grand Duke Murat as side A's commander and General of Infantry Prince Hohenlohe as side B's.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed commanders. Murat's letter and Höpfner's account agree that Murat commanded the French before Prenzlau and that Hohenlohe accepted the capitulation (claims side-a-command, side-b-command). English rendering (ours): as in claim bodart-strength.

claims.value: Murat, by his own account, had foreseen Hohenlohe's march and sent Lasalle to Prenzlau in the night; he ordered the attack on the suburb, had Boussard's brigade cross by a ford and Grouchy charge at its head, then brought up guns and sent General Belliard to summon Hohenlohe while his dragoons broke the Stettin gate. Grouchy says he had the town's gates broken with axes and at once had Hohenlohe summoned. Höpfner describes the French working on the Prussian command: a parlementaire, claiming to come from Bernadotte, said the Grand Duke stood near with 30,000 men and Lannes with 60,000 between Stettin and Prenzlau, so that escape was out of the question; Murat, using every means to convince Hohenlohe, gave him his word of honour that he was surrounded by a hundred thousand men, pointing out where the corps of Lannes, Bernadotte and Soult were supposed to stand; and a Frenchman passed off the smoke of a Prussian powder cart that had blown up by chance as Soult's signal.
claims.rationale: Murat's and Grouchy's letters and the parlementaire's claims from the page images; the rest of Höpfner from the OCR. Murat's bluff and the parlementaire's figures are their claims, not counts (claim side-b-information). English renderings (ours): Murat, as in claim side-b-strength for the heading and date; 'as I had foreseen, he had manoeuvred by my left, and had moved on Prenzlow after marching all night'; as in claim side-a-strength for Lasalle's night march and the attack on the suburb; 'seeing that the column was on the point of escaping me, I had General Boussard's brigade cross at a ford and ordered General Grouchy to charge at its head on the enemy'; 'I had cannon brought up, and sent General Belliard to summon Prince Hohenlohe. Meanwhile the dragoons broke in the Stettin gate and were about to debouch on the enemy when this Prince agreed to lay down his arms'; Grouchy, as in claim side-a-strength for the heading and date; 'the artillery was taken, the gunners cut down and the enemy pursued into the town, whose gates I had broken in with axes by our sappers, under the very fire of the Prussians'; 'taking advantage of the terror that such a success inspired in the enemy, I at once had Prince Hohenlohe summoned to surrender; he entered into parley, and soon Your Imperial Highness imposed on him the laws of war'; Höpfner, 'he claimed to have been sent by Marshal Bernadotte, and stated: the Grand Duke of Berg stood close by with 30,000 men and Marshal Lannes was already between Stettin and Prenzlau with 60,000 men, so that escape was accordingly no longer to be thought of; peace was moreover being negotiated'; 'the Grand Duke used every means to convince the Prince of the awkwardness of his situation' (OCR); 'I give you my word of honour that you are surrounded by a hundred thousand men' (OCR); 'and pointed out very vividly, gesticulating with his hands, the various places where the whole French army was supposed to stand' (OCR); 'the corps of Marshal Lannes! There is the corps of Marshal Bernadotte! There is the corps of Marshal Soult!' (OCR); 'ah, there is the signal of Marshal Soult' (OCR); 'that ball of smoke was nothing other than a Prussian powder cart which had blown up by chance without a loud report; the Frenchman had only been cunning enough to turn this to his advantage' (OCR).

claims.value: Höpfner: General Tschammer was charged with the defence of the approaches to Prenzlau; his companies and battalion guns covered the Berliner-Damm while two companies held the Berliner-Thor. He told the first parlementaire that he would continue his march without firing first, but whispered to General Hirschfeld that they were surrounded, and let Colonel Massenbach ride back with the parlementaire to see the enemy for himself. An officer of his suite, whose name was not established, ordered the grenadier battalion Dohna and the Wobeser dragoons back behind the town; Major Dohna left the gate despite Colonel Böhmke's order, and what caused this retreat Höpfner could not establish. Massenbach reported that they were not yet turned but might be in a few moments, that the Stettin road was open to the enemy and the enemy in the town, and urged that only pride and ambition could sacrifice the 7—8000 men still under the Prince's command; he assured General Hirschfeld that they were enclosed. Hohenlohe paid little attention to Captain Schöler's report and rode to meet Belliard; Hirschfeld was against any capitulation, and when Rittmeister Marwitz proposed falling on the small body standing in front, the Prince answered that Marshal Soult stood there. He reserved the terms for his generals and staff officers and obtained a longer truce. Before them he declared them surrounded and the road to Stettin cut, as Massenbach had seen for himself; Colonel Hüser, his chief of artillery, reported a want of ammunition, the guns having on average only 5—8 rounds, though he had only the battalion guns in view; the Prince called it his duty to accept the terms, all were silent, and he ordered the terms announced to the troops. Höpfner judges that the generals and staff officers were so blinded by Massenbach's false report and Hüser's misunderstood one that none rose to propose the most natural course, though most were men of the highest sense of honour, courage and talent.

claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Prenzlau on 28 October: the French under Murat forced the Prussian army under Hohenlohe to capitulate. Murat wrote the same day that Hohenlohe and his corps were in his power: the officers were prisoners of war, keeping their swords and baggage and free to go home until exchanged; the troops laid down their arms, were prisoners of war and were sent to France. Höpfner gives the terms the Prince announced: the officers to keep their swords, horses and equipages and the men their knapsacks; the officers released on their word of honour not to serve until exchanged; the Guards and the King's regiment to be quartered at Potsdam; the NCOs and men of all other troops to go to France until exchanged; the arms not to be laid down but only stacked. The arms were stacked and the cavalry dismounted while the French shouted 'Vive l'Empereur!'.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Murat's letter, read from the page image, and the terms in Höpfner (OCR); no source read gives a different result. The two accounts of the terms differ in detail (Höpfner's terms send the Guards and the King's regiment to Potsdam and have the arms stacked rather than laid down; Murat has the troops lay down their arms and go to France), and are not reconciled here. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Murat, as in claim side-b-strength for the heading and date; 'Sire, Your Majesty's orders are carried out. The Prince of Hohenlohe is in my power, as is his army corps'; 'the officers are prisoners of war, keep their swords and baggage and may return home until the exchange; the troops have laid down their arms, are prisoners of war and are sent back to France'; Höpfner, 'the officers keep their swords, horses and equipages, the common soldier his knapsack' (OCR); 'the officers are released on their word of honour not to serve until the exchange, and are free to go wherever they think fit' (OCR); 'to the royal Guards, as to His Majesty the King's regiment, although this is already captured, Potsdam shall be assigned as residence' (OCR); 'the NCOs and privates of all other troops shall be taken back to France until the exchange' (OCR); 'the muskets shall not be laid down but only stacked, the troops march off and leave them' (OCR); 'the thing was done! The officers rode to their units; the muskets were stacked; the cavalry dismounted, while the French opposite filled the air with wild music and the cry: "Vive l'Empereur!"'.

claims.value: Side B's loss: Bodart has 10,000 men (among them 400 officers) taken prisoner and 45 flags, 64 guns and 1,800 horses fallen to the French. Höpfner puts the troops that fell to the enemy by the capitulation itself at probably not over 10,000 men and 1800 horses. In the fighting before it the King's regiment, 25 officers and 701 men, fell into the enemy's power in the suburb; the grenadier company Taubenheim, 3 officers and 138 men, was partly cut down, partly taken, and General Tschammer with it; the Prittwitz dragoons, 375 horses strong, lost 2 officers and 20 dragoons killed and 5 officers, 97 dragoons and 120 horses wounded and captured; Lieutenants Linstow II and Rothkirch II of those dragoons fell and 7 officers were wounded; and the horse battery Studnitz-Schorlemmer was lost but for 2 guns. Of the captured men surely half ran off from the first night quarters. Side A's figures: Murat has Grouchy take 18 guns before the gates were shut and gives the result of the day as 16,000 infantry, 6 regiments of cavalry, 60 guns and 60 flags; Grouchy reports a general officer, several flags and standards and 8 guns with their caissons taken in the suburb.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, not combined: Bodart's 10,000 men and 1,800 horses are Höpfner's estimate for the capitulation itself, his 45 flags and 64 guns the French reports' figures as Höpfner gives them (claim side-b-strength-french), and his 400 officers are not Höpfner's tabulated 300 (claim side-b-strength). The losses in the fighting before the capitulation are Höpfner's separate figures, from the page images of pp. 185 and 197; the Taubenheim company's fate, General Tschammer's capture and the runaways are from the OCR. The two lieutenants killed and the 7 officers wounded are not combined with the Prittwitz regiment's loss. claims.value: Bodart places Prenzlau in Brandenburg at the outflow of the Ucker from the Uckersee, 120 km north-east of Potsdam. Höpfner: the Ucker, fordable in many places, is a considerable obstacle for its broad marshy meadows; the two roads into the town on the left bank of the Ucker each crossed a long dam running straight to the town gates, which and could easily be defended by artillery fire; the Strom or Gollmitz brook covered the Prussian right flank with its high left bank and marshy surroundings, but had several cavalry fords near Prenzlau; and the defile of Prenzlau, which could not be turned for a long way on either side, made an excellent defensive position for an army retreating on Löcknitz. Grouchy saw Hohenlohe's column from heights dominating the town; a marsh that Hohenlohe believed covered his column's march had a practicable passage; Prussian infantry held the orchards left of the road; and guns swept the main street of the suburb. Prince August, cut off, gained heights that offered him an advantageous position, and was driven from them into a marsh (Murat).

claims.value: Side B: Höpfner says the troops were exhausted by forced marches for 14 days, the last of them lasting 36 hours; almost all had been without food for those 36 hours, and the horses were worn out. claims.value: Side B was misled. Captain Tippelskirch reported nothing of the enemy beyond Prenzlau. A parlementaire who said he came from Bernadotte claimed that Murat stood near with 30,000 men and Lannes with 60,000 between Stettin and Prenzlau, and that peace was being negotiated. Colonel Massenbach, sent back with him to see the enemy for himself, took the crossing he reached for the Seehausen defile in his excited imagination, and reported that he had spoken with Marshals Murat and Lannes, whose corps must be near; Höpfner cites fairly reliable reports that Lannes came to Templin only later and left it for Prenzlau only in the night, so that Massenbach would seem to have been mystified. Murat claimed a hundred thousand men, and a Frenchman passed off the smoke of an exploding Prussian powder cart as Soult's signal. Captain Tippelskirch, who had ridden off towards Löcknitz, met peasants from Stettin who had heard nothing of the enemy on the whole road, but instead of bringing back the news he stopped to feed his horses.
claims.rationale: Side B's history; Tippelskirch's first report, the parlementaire's claims and Massenbach's from the page images of pp. 181 and 189, the rest from the OCR. English renderings (ours): 'Captain Tippelskirch, who, as mentioned, had ridden ahead to Prenzlau, came back with the report that nothing of the enemy was to be seen beyond Prenzlau'; as in claim side-a-command for the parlementaire's statement; 'verbatim extract from Massenbach's historical' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for Massenbach's ride; 'for in his excited imagination he took the crossing — probably the one at the Tissort mill — for the defile of Seehausen' (OCR); 'Marshals Murat and Lannes spoken with. Their corps must be near'; 'according to other fairly reliable reports Marshal Lannes came to Templin only on the ... and left there for Prenzlau only in the night at ... o'clock, so that it would appear that Colonel Massenbach had been mystified' (OCR); as in claim side-a-command for Murat's word of honour and the powder cart (OCR); 'Captain Tippelskirch, who, as mentioned above, had ridden in the direction of Löcknitz' (OCR); 'when he met several peasants with empty carts who stated that they had driven out of Stettin in the night, and declared unanimously that they had heard nothing whatever of the enemy on the whole way' (OCR); 'instead of turning back at once and bringing the Prince this most important news, the captain had his horses fed' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B was retreating on Stettin by Löcknitz: Höpfner calls the defile of Prenzlau an excellent defensive position for an army retreating on Löcknitz; Hohenlohe told the first parlementaire that he would continue his march and let it come to a meeting with an enemy corps before Stettin; General Tschammer was to hold until Prince August's grenadier battalion, the rear guard with the King's regiment, had come up; and behind the town the infantry was to fall back by brigades en échiquier. Before the council the Prince said that by his own feeling he would rather die arms in hand than stain his fame with a capitulation, but that he would not uselessly sacrifice so many men to his fame when the terms offered could preserve them for the fatherland.
claims.rationale: Side B's history; Höpfner's account of the position from the page image of p. 186, the rest from the OCR. English renderings (ours): as in claim prenzlau-ground for the defile (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the answer to the parlementaire; 'General Tschammer now received command of the rear guard, and the Prince expressly ordered him to hold until Prince August with his grenadier battalion, which with the King's regiment had formed the rear guard of the column, had arrived' (OCR); 'in the position behind Prenzlau the infantry that had happily got back stood in hollow squares astride the road to Pasewalk and facing the town'; 'the cavalry behind and between the squares. The infantry was to retire by brigades en échiquier'; 'by his personal feeling he would prefer to die with arms in hand rather than at his age still stain his fame with the shame of a capitulation' (OCR); 'but when he considered that he was to sacrifice uselessly to his fame alone the lives of so many people who, by the terms the enemy offered him, could be preserved for the fatherland, he believed that it was honest dealing to sacrifice his fame to the general welfare' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A attacked: Murat ordered Lasalle to attack the suburb, the dragoons charged the Prussian rear guard and forced their way to the gates, and the French then summoned the army behind the town. Side B covered its passage through the defile with troops posted at the dam and the gate, and stood in position behind the town; when Rittmeister Marwitz proposed falling on the small body of French in front, the Prince pointed to Marshal Soult.
claims.rationale: Both sides' accounts describe the French attacking and side B defending and then capitulating. The attack on the suburb was Murat's own order on the field, by his letter, so the claim is tagged commander_created. claims.value: Side B used the town's enclosure to check the pursuit. Höpfner: the new town of Prenzlau on the left bank of the Ucker had only a palisade, the old town on the right bank a mostly well-preserved, strong wall; grenadiers held the Berliner-Thor, whose leaves Major Dohna closed, ending the pursuit there, and sharpshooters stayed to hold a gap in the wall beside the gate, closed only with palisades, which the enemy tried to force; Captain Brünnow says he began his retreat from the gate only when the enemy light infantry had already come over the low town wall and the barrier. Murat says the gates were shut against Grouchy and his dragoons broke in the Stettin gate; Grouchy that his sappers broke the gates with axes under Prussian fire. The army capitulated in the open position behind the town.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: the town's wall, palisades and gates existed before the action and side B held them against side A's pursuit, so the claim is tagged inherited. A coding that counted only the position where the army capitulated, in the open behind the town, would give none_named. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the new town of Prenzlau on the left bank of the Ucker had only a palisade, but the old town on the right bank a mostly well-preserved, strong wall' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the companies at the Berliner-Thor; 'at the Berliner-Thor the fire of the grenadiers put an end to the pursuit; Major Count Dohna succeeded in closing the gate leaves'; 'only Lieutenant Seydlitz with the sharpshooters of the battalion Dohna remained at the gate, to occupy the gap in the wall at the side, which was closed only with the help of palisades and into which the enemy tried to force his way' (OCR); as in claim side-a-strength for Brünnow's report (OCR and image); Murat, as in claims side-b-strength for the heading and date, side-b-losses for the gates shut and side-a-command for the Stettin gate; Grouchy, as in claims side-a-strength for the heading and date and side-a-command for the axes; Höpfner, as in claim side-b-objectives for the position behind the town.

open_questions: Deferred: Höpfner's account of Prince August's battalion and the Quitzow cuirassiers (from p. 198); Massenbach's memoir and the Marwitz and Hohenlohe reports that Höpfner quotes or cites; the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests; a French return of prisoners, guns and flags; the Bulletin's account of Prenzlau. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the dams' length and the distances in Höpfner's description of the ground (pp. 177-178), the patrols' strengths (p. 179), the French battery and the Prussian half battery (pp. 182-183), the hour of the French attack and the squadrons and companies in the suburb fight (pp. 183-184), Massenbach's enemy strength (p. 190), the distances and days of a retreat to Stettin (p. 195), and the date and hour of Lannes's arrival at Templin (p. 187).

Most consequential gap: side B's strength and loss at the capitulation, given as Höpfner's table of 300 officers, 8831 men and 1616 horses with units unaccounted for, his estimate of not over 10,000 men and 1800 horses, Bodart's 10,000 with 400 officers, and Murat's 16,000 infantry and 6 cavalry regiments; a French return of the prisoners or the sources of Höpfner's table could settle it. The guns are similarly uncertain (64 horsed guns in the French reports Höpfner cites and in Bodart, 60 in Murat's letter, 30 actually handed over or taken besides the regimental guns by Höpfner).

Disputes kept as separate claims: the Prussian strength and prisoners (Höpfner's table and estimate; Bodart's 10,000 with 400 officers; Murat's 16,000 infantry and 6 cavalry regiments; Milhaud's informants' 18,000 and 36 guns; Massenbach's 7-8000); guns and flags (Bodart's 64 and 45; Murat's 60 and 60; Murat's 18 guns taken by Grouchy; Grouchy's 8 guns in the suburb; Höpfner's 30 besides the regimental guns); the terms (prisoners of war in Murat, released on parole in Höpfner; arms laid down in Murat, only stacked in Höpfner); whether Lannes's corps was near (the parlementaire's and Murat's claims, Taubenheim's voltigeurs, Höpfner's note on Lannes's arrival at Templin).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 10,000 men and 1,800 horses are Höpfner's estimate and his 45 flags and 64 guns the French reports' figures as Höpfner gives them); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Milhaud's note, Murat's letter to the Emperor and Grouchy's report to Murat); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history, from reports including Massenbach's, Marwitz's and Hohenlohe's, which he quotes or cites).
